arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Shay Dvoretzky argued for Samantar. He stated that the Act applies to officials acting on the state's behalf. He claimed such suits are equivalent to suing the state directly.
Paula Millett argued for Yousuf. She contended the Act was not intended to apply to preexisting common law. She argued the statute does not create a blanket exception for officials.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act. The Act generally blocks suits against foreign states. It does not explicitly mention individual officials. The core dispute is whether suing an official counts as suing the state.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Samantar wants the court to dismiss the lawsuit. He argues the Act grants him immunity as a state agent.
Yousuf wants the lawsuit to proceed. He argues the Act does not protect individual officials from personal liability.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Samantar argues that suits against officials acting for the state are equivalent to suits against the state itself.
Yousuf argues that the Act was not intended to replace the preexisting common law of official immunity.

Justice Kennedy asked what legal authority supports the proposition that the Act covers officials.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between state and individual liability. It determines whether victims can sue foreign officials directly. It shapes the reach of international human rights law in U.S. courts.
